a.summary: A newly documented caller-visible array-ownership surprise was added at the declaration but not to CONVENTIONS.md, the file whose stated purpose is to make that family visible in one place.
a.failure_scenario: A consumer follows the file's own instruction ("Read this before writing assertions against an API you have not used here") and reads the `## Byte-array ownership` section. It tells them which factories retain an input array and that they can pass `bytes.clone()`. It says nothing about a factory that reorders an input array. They call the four-arg `createTx` with a reused `sortedAccounts`, reuse it afterward, and get the wrong account order — the exact behavior the delta just documented and that uses the same `clone()` remedy the section already teaches.

b.summary: CONVENTIONS.md's array-ownership family was not extended with the newly documented caller-array mutation, so the file's stated guarantee that the family is 'visible in one place' no longer holds for the behaviour this delta just established as a published contract.
b.failure_scenario: A consumer following the repo's own stated navigation reads CONVENTIONS.md's 'Byte-array ownership' section to learn which sava APIs take ownership of caller-supplied arrays. It tells them createPubKey/createDiscriminator retain their input and that they can pass bytes.clone(). It says nothing about Transaction.createTx permuting a caller-supplied AccountMeta[] in place. They conclude no other array-ownership hazard exists, pass their own sorted array to createTx, reuse it, and get the permutation described in the finding above. The file's premise — that it exists so the family is visible in one place — is what makes the omission actively misleading rather than merely incomplete.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.

claims_new_evidence.instructions: Does `b` cite evidence that `a` does not?

criteria.true: `b` names a file, test, command, observation, or reproduction that `a` does not mention.
criteria.false: `b` cites nothing beyond what `a` already cites, or cites nothing at all.
